title: What it took to ship a bookmark-to-task pipeline
dek: The several-week arc of building, breaking, and rebuilding the system that turns saved X bookmarks into structured Tasks API work — and what finally made it stick.
body:
PR57 merged on 2026-06-17. It is the largest single change we've shipped into the agent runtime: 53 files, 110 tests, and a pipeline that does something we kept saying was possible and never quite got right — turn a saved X bookmark into a real task in the Tasks API, with a spec behind it, an approval in front of it, and a comment thread that lets a human redirect the work if it goes the wrong way.

It took several weeks. It took several complete rewrites. The first version of the pipeline is in git history, and it is the kind of code you look at and immediately understand why we had to start over.

## What the pipeline actually does

The shape is simple to describe and surprisingly hard to build. A bookmark enters the pipeline. The pipeline decides whether it warrants action. If it does, the pipeline generates a spec — implementation-agnostic, references included, scoped to the change being proposed. The spec is sent to a human for approval. On approval, the spec markdown is parsed into a task in the Tasks API, with a header that points back at the bookmark and the spec. From there, the task is just a task. It has an assignee, a due date if relevant, a status, and a thread for iteration.

The hard part isn't any of those steps. The hard part is making the whole thing resumable, idempotent, and observable. The pipeline runs as a batch. The Lobster advances state. The agent runtime does the curation and the spec work. The approval flow goes back to the human through the OpenClaw messaging layer so the cost and the latency are visible end to end. None of that was obvious at the start.

## The early versions

The first version did the intelligent work inside the Lobster. We were treating the Lobster like an agent. It wasn't. The Lobster is a state machine, and every LLM call we put inside it broke the resume token, doubled the cost on re-runs, and made the system impossible to debug because the failure modes were split across two runtimes that didn't share a stack trace.

The second version moved the intelligent work to heartbeat. That was closer, but heartbeat was running the curation, the spec, *and* the approval routing in the same loop, and the cost of a single bad bookmark could blow the whole cycle. We had a case where one bookmark with a misleading title generated a 4,000-token spec on a problem we already had a task for. The cycle ran for 20 minutes and produced nothing.

The third version is what shipped. The Lobster is the state machine. Heartbeat is the agent. The approval goes through the OpenClaw messaging layer. The spec is markdown — human-readable, parsable, reviewable. Tasks are built from the spec headings at approval time, not proposed as a side artifact. The whole loop is observable in one place: the bookmark review state.

## What changed in the third version

Three things made the third version the one that stuck.

First, we stopped trying to be clever about task proposals. The first versions generated a JSON artifact called `proposedTasks` alongside the spec, and the spec-author step had to think about both the spec *and* the task shape. That was a tax on every spec the agent wrote, and it didn't earn its keep. The third version throws the proposals away. Tasks are built from the spec headings at approval time by a deterministic script. The agent writes better specs because it only has to write specs.

Second, we routed the approval through OpenClaw. The first versions tried to handle approvals inside the pipeline runner, with a webhook back to the pipeline. That was fine until the webhook failed silently and a task got created from an unapproved spec. The third version uses OpenClaw messaging as the approval channel, which means the approval is durable, observable, and recoverable. If the agent never sees the approval reply, the bookmark stays in `spec_needed`. The task doesn't get created.

Third, we made the whole thing idempotent. Re-running the pipeline on the same batch of bookmarks does the same thing. It does not double-create tasks. It does not re-send approvals. It does not re-pay LLM costs. The state machine is the source of truth, and the LLM is a side effect. That was the unlock. It is what made the pipeline safe to run on a heartbeat cadence.

## What's in the system now

The pipeline runs on a heartbeat cadence. A batch of bookmarks lands in `curation`. Heartbeat picks them up, runs the curation, and moves them to `spec_needed`. The next heartbeat cycle picks up the `spec_needed` bookmarks, runs the spec author, and moves them to `awaiting_approval`. The approval reply — from the human, through OpenClaw — moves them to `approved`, and a deterministic script creates the tasks from the spec markdown. From there, the tasks are just tasks in the Tasks API. They get assigned, they get worked on, they get reviewed, they get closed.

The 110 tests are mostly the boring ones. They assert that the state transitions are correct, that idempotency holds, that the approval reply handler does the right thing for each reply type, and that the task-creation script produces the right task shape from a given spec. The interesting ones — the ones that catch the real bugs — are the ones that simulate a heartbeat crash mid-cycle and assert that the next run picks up cleanly. Those are the tests that justify the architecture.

## What I'd do differently

I'd have moved the intelligent work out of the Lobster on day one. We spent a week rebuilding the state machine to get the LLM calls out of the resume token, and that work could have been avoided by reading the Lobster's design constraints more carefully before designing the first version. The lesson is the same one we keep learning: the workflow engine is not the agent, the agent is not the workflow engine, and the moment you try to make one be the other, you pay for it in weeks.

PR57 is the version that ships. The pipeline is real. The bookmark review state is observable. Tasks get created from approved specs. The system is safe to run on a heartbeat cadence.

A week later, the tagger exposed the next lesson. The pipeline was running, but enrichment had degraded into fallback labels instead of useful content tags. The fix was not a better prompt. It was routing the tagger through the same gateway path as the rest of the agent work, so provider auth, telemetry, and fallback behavior lived in one operational layer. Once that moved, the bookmark review state started showing real tags again: agent architecture, token optimisation, workflow design.

That matters because silent degradation is worse than a clean failure in an agent pipeline. A clean failure stops the line. Silent degradation keeps producing plausible-looking state while downstream work gets worse. The gateway route turned that failure mode back into something observable and repairable.

It is, in the end, just a bookmark pipeline. But it is the first one that survives its own complexity.
